## Claims — §II (1:3–14), grouped by pericope

### 1:3 — Berakah opening / "spiritual blessings in the heavenly places"
- **[1:3]** The opening follows a **traditional Jewish benedictory pattern** (bless God because God has given blessings). Thielman (primary-pattern data): "The opening line of Paul's benediction follows a pattern familiar from Israel's Scriptures and Jewish literature of the Second Temple period" (Gen. 24:27; Jdt. 13:18; Tob. 13:17; 4Q404 10).
- **[1:3]** εὐλογητός (*eulogētos*) is a **verbal adjective** meaning "blessed" in the sense of "praised." Thielman: "Paul is saying that God is praised by those whom he has blessed. He is not expressing the wish that God would be blessed" — analogous to Rom. 1:25 (*hos estin eulogētos*).
- **[1:3]** In **non-Jewish** Greek, εὐλογέω/εὐλογία referred to praising *people* ("speak well of," panegyric, eulogy; gods "blessing" = only "honoring," LSJ 720); Paul instead follows **Biblical Greek**, where the terms denote "the good things that God does for them" (Gen. 14:20; Exod. 18:10; Ruth 4:14; Jdt. 13:18). Thielman's own synthesis.
- **[1:3]** πνευματικός (*pneumatikos*, "spiritual") — Thielman's own view (against a patristic/otherworldly reading): "When Paul uses the adjective πνευματικός…God's Spirit almost always stands in the background." So **"spiritual blessings" = benefits that come as gracious gifts from the Spirit of God** (citing Fee 1994:28–32; Aletti 2001:56), NOT "nonmaterial/otherworldly" blessings (the latter attributed to "many interpreters in the early church, and some in more recent times").
- **[1:3]** ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις (*en tois epouraniois*, "in the heavenly places") — phrase unique to Ephesians in NT (1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12); Thielman: refers to "the location or, perhaps better, the 'dimension' of existence in which believers experience 'every spiritual blessing'" — a realm where God, the ascended Christ, AND "the spiritual powers of evil" dwell (citing W.H. Harris 1991; Hanson 1980).
- **[1:3]** ἐν Χριστῷ (*en Christō*) "refers even more specifically to the place where these blessings are found…within the boundaries marked out by the living Christ" — the realm of hearing/believing the gospel and being sealed with the Spirit (1:13).

### 1:4 — Election (ἐξελέξατο) before the foundation of the world
- **[1:4]** καθώς (*kathōs*, "inasmuch as") — normally comparison, can be causal; Thielman: "notions of comparison are probably uppermost," God blessed "to the extent that" he gave lavish blessings (citing Ellicott, Eadie, Schlier).
- **[1:4]** ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς (*exelexato hēmas*, "he chose us") is **the only main/finite verb in vv. 3–14** not subordinate to another element (citing Hoehner 2002:175); Thielman: this grammatical priority "probably" = conceptual priority — God's free choice is "the clearest indicator of the lavish nature of his grace."
- **[1:4]** God's choice is a **traditional Jewish idea** rooted in Scripture (Deut. 14:2; Isa. 43:10); nothing in Israel (size, righteousness) prompted it — only God's love (Deut. 7:7–8). Paul elsewhere: God chose not by merit (Rom. 9:11–12; 1 Cor. 1:27–29; 2 Tim. 1:9; Titus 1:1–2) and links election to love (Rom. 8:33–39; 1 Thess. 1:4).
- **[1:4]** ἐν αὐτῷ (*en autō*, "in him") — Thielman's own view: **does NOT refer to Christ's preexistence** (rejecting Pokorný 1992:57 "among many others"); rather, like *dia Iēsou Christou* in v. 5, it "describes the means by which God's choice became effective for believers" through Christ's death (v. 7a) — citing Oecumenius, Cambier.
- **[1:4]** πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου (*pro katabolēs kosmou*, "before the foundation of the world") — a common Second-Temple/early-Christian phrase for creation; the idea that God chose his people before the world's foundation was "well known." Thielman: Paul uses it "to emphasize the graciousness of God's choice: it happened before believers could do anything to effect it" (Calvin, Best, O'Brien).
- **[1:4]** ἁγίους καὶ ἀμώμους (*hagious kai amōmous*, "holy and blameless") — election language of Deut. 7:1–6; ἄμωμος is LXX sacrificial-cult language ("unblemished" animal, Exod./Lev./Num.), used metaphorically ("morally blameless"); κατενώπιον αὐτοῦ ("before him") keeps the sacrificial metaphor alive (κατενώπιον also cultic in Lev. 4:17; Best 1998:121).
- **[1:4]** ἐν ἀγάπῃ (*en agapē*, "in love") — a genuine syntactic crux (see Key Exegetical Decisions). Thielman's own conclusion: it attaches to "holy and blameless" (describing believers' conduct), NOT to *proorisas* in v. 5. This makes the benediction **anticipate the ethical exhortation of 4:1–6:20** ("bear with one another in love," 4:2).

### 1:5 — Predestination to adoptive sonship (proorisas / huiothesia)
- **[1:5a]** προορίσας (*proorisas*, "having predestined") — πρό prefixed to ὁρίζω ("determine") to place God's decision "chronologically before the world began." Thielman treats *proorisas hēmas* as a **restatement** of *exelexato hēmas*, not a distinct logical step: "Paul simply turns the jewel slightly and views it from a different angle." He declines the philosophical logic-of-election debate (contrasts with what "one of these explanations might be correct" if Paul were doing philosophy à la Calvin).
- **[1:5a]** υἱοθεσία (*huiothesia*, "adoptive sonship") — a **distinctively Pauline term** in the Greek Bible: never in LXX; in NT only here + Gal. 4:5; Rom. 8:15, 23; 9:4. Greco-Roman legal practice (father accepts a non-biological male child as heir); Gentile readers in Roman Asia would hear this, but Paul also draws on **biblical Israel-as-son** ideas (Rom. 9:4; citing J. Scott 1992; Byrne 1979).
- **[1:5a]** OT/Second-Temple call Israel God's "sons"/"children"/"firstborn son" (Deut. 14:1; Exod. 4:22–23; etc.); relationship strained by rebellion, to be restored eschatologically. Thielman: the Spirit's presence = evidence eschatological restoration has begun; believers are God's children, spiritually related to Jesus (Son *par excellence*), heirs of future glory completed at bodily resurrection (Gal. 4:1–7; Rom. 8:14–17).
- **[1:5a]** διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (*dia Iēsou Christou*) — adoption is "through Jesus Christ" because "through their union with him, Jesus Christ shares his divine sonship with them"; believers call God "Abba Father" because Jesus did (Gal. 4:6; Rom. 8:15; Mark 14:36; Jeremias 1971).
- **[1:5a]** εἰς αὐτόν (*eis auton*, "to/for him[self]") — αὐτόν could be Christ or God; Thielman decides **God** (following the pattern action→purpose→divine goal): "the goal of the adoptive sonship of believers is a relationship with God similar to that of Jesus's own filial relationship with God."
- **[1:5b]** κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ (*eudokia*, "good pleasure of his will") — Paul was "not content to say simply that God predestined…according to his will"; εὐδοκία expresses "deep desire," "great pleasure" (Barth, Best).

### 1:6 — "praise of his glorious grace…in the Beloved"
- **[1:6]** εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ — the string of genitives is typical of the letter's first-half style; genitive strings "slow the discourse and emphasize the grandeur or gravity of the thought" (1:18b, 19b; 2:2b; etc.).
- **[1:6]** ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ (*en tō ēgapēmenō*, "in the Beloved") — picks up *en Christō* (v.3), *en autō* (v.4), *dia Iēsou Christou* (v.5). "Beloved" title: Scripture/Second-Temple call great individuals (Abraham, Moses, Solomon) and **Israel itself** "beloved" (Jeshurun rendered "beloved" in LXX); Synoptics call Jesus "Beloved" (Matt. 3:17 etc.). Thielman's own view (citing Caird, Lincoln, O'Brien): calling Jesus "the Beloved" evokes "Jesus's embodiment within himself of the beloved and elect people of God" — grace given not merely "by means of" but "in the Beloved," through identification with Christ.
- **[1:6 Additional Note — text-critical]** Variant τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ **ἐν ᾗ** ἐχαρίτωσεν vs. **ἧς** ἐχαρίτωσεν. Thielman: ἧς is original (earliest MSS 𝔓46, א*, A, B, P; consistent with letter's style in vv.7–8), rejecting ἐν ᾗ (adopted by Hoehner 2002:202). ἐν ᾗ would lend itself to "he made us gracious by his grace" (Chrysostom's direction, though Chrysostom read ἧς).
- **[1:6 Additional Note]** Variant adding υἱῷ αὐτοῦ after ἠγαπημένῳ (D*, F, G; Augustine, Pelagius, Ambrosiaster) — Thielman: "very weak support," Western, late; the phrase is a scribal import from Col. 1:13. Not authentic.

### 1:7–8 — Redemption through his blood / forgiveness (apolytrōsis)
- **[1:7a]** ἐν ᾧ (*en hō*) = "in whom," NOT "by whom" — "God made believers his people through their identification with Christ" (Abbott, Best, Hoehner; *pace* Calvin, Alford).
- **[1:7a]** ἀπολύτρωσις (*apolytrōsis*, "redemption") — appears only 10× in NT, rare in pre-NT Greek; LXX Dan. 4:34 ≈ "deliverance"; non-biblical Greek = "holding/paying a ransom," freeing slaves by a price (Plutarch, Josephus, Let. Aris., Philo).
- **[1:7a — the ransom debate]** Thielman reports a "heated debate": (1) *apolytrōsis* = specific purchase of people from captivity to sin at the cost of Christ's death (Morris 1955; Ridderbos), reading διὰ τοῦ αἵματος as the ransom price; vs. (2) general deliverance from sin's plight (Abbott; Büchsel TDNT; D. Hill 1967), arguing διά + genitive = means only, not price (Best, Lincoln). Photius (9th c.) cited for the ransom view ("giving his blood as a ransom [*lytron*]…he ransomed us from the tyranny").
- **[1:7a — Thielman's own adjudication]** He clears the "theological air": the NT unambiguously calls Christ's blood a ransom price (1 Pet. 1:18–19; Heb. 9:12; Rev. 1:5; 5:9). He concludes the slave-redemption/price metaphor was **"alive for" Paul** and his Gentile readers would hear διὰ τοῦ αἵματος as purchase price — BUT Paul's **primary** concern was the biblical overtone of God's great deliverance/rescue of his people (as from Egypt/Babylon), citing λυτρόω / *gāʾal* / *pādâ* usage (Exod. 6:6). This "accounts better" for the future-broadening of the word in 1:14 and 4:30.
- **[1:7a]** ἄφεσις τῶν παραπτωμάτων (*aphesis*, "forgiveness of transgressions") — ἄφεσις only 2× in Paul (here + Col. 1:14); forgiveness words are rare in Paul but the concept is latent in his justification/reconciliation language (Rom. 4:7–8; 2 Cor. 5:19). Redemption "entailed" forgiveness (apposition).
- **[1:7b–8]** κατὰ τὸ πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ ("according to the wealth of his grace") + ἐπερίσσευσεν (*eperisseusen*, "lavished/caused to abound") — God "not merely showed…grace…he also 'caused' grace 'to abound.'"
- **[1:8b — crux]** ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει ("in all wisdom and understanding") — Thielman follows the **minority position: this = GOD's wisdom**, not a gift of wisdom to believers. He applies Occam's razor / first-hearer perspective and the v.6b parallel (Alford). He also decides it modifies **ἐπερίσσευσεν** (preceding) rather than γνωρίσας (following), on the ground that adverbial prepositional phrases in 1:3–14 mostly follow their verbs. Result: God's grace-lavishing was "not a haphazard or ill-considered action" but "in accord with his infinite capacity for wisdom and understanding." (Majority view — that it's a gift of wisdom to believers, per Eph. 1:17–18; Col. 1:9 — is reported and set aside.)

### 1:9–10 — The mystērion: to sum up all things in Christ (anakephalaiōsasthai)
- **[1:9]** γνωρίσας (*gnōrisas*, "making known") is dependent on ἐπερίσσευσεν — "does not…signal a new step in the argument" (*pace* Caragounis, Best); revealing the mystery is another way God's grace abounded.
- **[1:9]** μυστήριον τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ — v.9 mirrors v.5's stylistic pattern (*proorisas*…*kata tēn eudokian tou thelēmatos* ∥ *gnōrisas*…*kata tēn eudokian autou hēn proetheto en autō*). προέθετο prefix προ- normally lacks "prior"-planning force, but Thielman thinks Paul intends temporal emphasis given the benediction's πρό-saturation (πρό v.4; προορίσας v.5; προορισθέντες/πρόθεσιν v.11; προηλπικότας v.12) — citing Schlier, Gnilka.
- **[1:10]** εἰς οἰκονομίαν τοῦ πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν ("for the administration of the fullness of the times") — Thielman: εἰς = "for the purpose of" (not "at the time of," *pace* Hoehner, or "in reference to," *pace* Eadie, Lightfoot); οἰκονομία = **God's work of administering** his plan (not Paul's administrative role, not the plan itself). Parallels Daniel's God who "changes times and seasons" (Dan. 2:21).
- **[1:10 — key term]** ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι (*anakephalaiōsasthai*, "to sum up") — Thielman rejects two "exegetical errors": (1) the ἀνά="re-" reading of Jerome/Theodoret/John of Damascus (recapitulation/restoration of fallen creation); (2) the κεφαλή="head" reading linking it to Christ's headship (1:22; 4:15; 5:23) — rejected because the word derives from κεφάλαιον ("main point"), not κεφαλή, and this is the first κεφαλ- occurrence in the letter, so readers couldn't retroject later headship theme. **Thielman's own view:** the common **rhetorical/literary** meaning — "recapitulation," summary gathering of scattered elements — is correct (Quintilian *Inst.* 6.1.1 "repetition and grouping of facts"; Dionysius of Halicarnassus; Rom. 13:9). So the mystery = "God's plan to sum up his disparate creation in Christ…Christ will emerge as the organizing principle of all creation." He cautions "we should not…get ahead of Paul" toward the later cosmic-subjection theme (1:20–22; cf. 1 Cor. 15:28; Phil. 2:10; Col. 1:20).
- **[1:9–10 Additional Note on μυστήριον]** Extended survey (Thielman reporting usage): Greco-Roman mystery cults (Eleusis; secret initiatory rites, Bornkamm TDNT); Hellenistic Jewish usage (Wisdom of Solomon; 1 Enoch cosmic secrets); **most characteristic Jewish use = Daniel's translation of Aramaic רָז (*rāz*)** — God's orchestration of the rise/fall of kingdoms toward "the last days" (Dan. 2:28–29; DSS; 2 Baruch, revealed "according to the multitude of his grace"). In undisputed Paul μυστήριον = esoteric-yet-non-merit-based knowledge (1 Cor. 4:1; 13:2; 14:2) and eschatological events (2 Thess. 2:7; Rom. 11:25; 1 Cor. 15:51; Col. 1:27). **In Ephesians specifically**, "this element of the mystery rises to prominence": the union of Jewish and Gentile believers in one body/church (Eph. 3:3–6; cf. 5:32). Here in 1:9 μυστήριον = "the knowledge that God intends to sum up all things in Christ."

### 1:11–12 — Made heirs / predestined / "we who hope beforehand"
- **[1:11]** Structural note: v.11 third section mirrors first section (choice/adoption vv.4–5 → heirship v.11; "good pleasure of his will" v.5 → "purpose…counsel of his will" v.11). Advances thought: children are also **heirs** (cf. Rom. 8:17), with **greater emphasis on the deliberate nature** of God's action.
- **[1:11]** ἐκληρώθημεν (*eklērōthēmen*) — verb κληρόω rare in Biblical Greek (only here, 1 Sam. 14:41, Isa. 17:11); normally "appoint by lot / allot." Options Thielman reports: (a) "we have been allotted [a destiny/lot]" (cf. Col. 1:12; Wis. 5:5; 1QS); (b) believers "allotted **to God** as his portion" like Israel (O'Brien; Robinson, Alford, Westcott). **Thielman's own view:** best taken via the cognate κληρονόμος/κληρονομία family = **"made heirs / given an inheritance"**; and (since v.14 speaks of believers' inheritance, cf. Rom. 8:17) the inheritance is **theirs**, not God's. "Here in 1:11, he praises God for making believers his heirs."
- **[1:11]** προορισθέντες (*prooristhentes*, "predestined," passive) parallels v.5's active προορίσας. Accent here on **God's meticulous, sovereign planning**: piled-up words πρόθεσις (*prothesis*, purpose), ἐνεργέω (*energeō*, work), βουλή (*boulē*, counsel), θέλημα (*thelēma*, will). Purpose: to make believers feel "an especially privileged people — privileged not because of their accomplishments (2:5, 8) but because of what God…has done." Not haphazard, not earned.
- **[1:12]** εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης αὐτοῦ ("that we might exist for the praise of his glory") — parallels v.6a.
- **[1:12 — crux]** τοὺς προηλπικότας ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ ("we who hope beforehand in Christ"). Thielman **rejects** the traditional Jewish/Jewish-Christian reading ("we Jews who hoped beforehand in the Messiah," contrasted with Gentile "you also" in v.13; attributed to "many interpreters," and Aletti 2001). Argument: Paul uses first-person plural "we" ~10× in the benediction for **all** Christians; the "we" of v.11 (*eklērōthēmen*) must match the "we" of v.7 (all who have redemption); and προορίζω appears in both v.5 and v.11 with the same referent. προηλπικότας (verb rare — only here in NT, never LXX) = "hope for before / anticipate"; its **perfect tense** emphasizes the present state of believers (citing Campbell 2008). The prefix **πρό refers to the present time "before" the consummation**, not to the past — "hope beforehand" = before the full summation of all things (v.10) — citing Haupt, Masson, *pace* Lindemann, Aletti.

### 1:13–14 — Sealing with the promised Holy Spirit / arrabōn
- **[1:13a]** ἐν ᾧ ("in whom") — the fourth "hinge" phrase (like vv.6b–7a, 10b–11a). Paul turns directly to readers ("you also") for the first time since the greeting (v.2). Thielman: NOT a Jew/Gentile contrast ("we Jews made heirs" vs. "you Gentiles sealed") — rather emphasizes that all the blessings of vv.4–12 "belong to them" personally. Possible pastoral purpose: if 3:13 hints the readers were **discouraged**, the benediction redirects their focus to God's blessings.
- **[1:13a — syntax]** The two adverbial clauses ("when you heard…the gospel of your salvation" / "when you believed") joined by no connective = an **anacoluthon** (broken sentence, common in Paul). Thielman: ἀκούσαντες and πιστεύσαντες are aorist adverbial participles of time referring not to a sequence but to **two aspects of one event**; and since the main verb ἐσφραγίσθητε is aorist, "hearing the gospel, believing it, and receiving the seal of the Holy Spirit all happened at once." Also: ἐν ᾧ in "when you believed" marks the **sphere** ("in Christ"), not Christ as object of faith.
- **[1:13a]** Gospel described as τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας ("word of truth") and τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῆς σωτηρίας ("gospel of salvation"). "Word of truth" may echo the true-vs-false-gospel contrast (Gal. 2:5, 14; Col. 1:5). σωτηρία: Thielman argues (against Muddiman, Mitton, Lindemann who read it as already-completed salvation à la 2:1–10) that here salvation is **future/hoped-for** (cf. v.12 hope, v.14 future inheritance/redemption; 1 Thess. 5:8–9).
- **[1:13b–14]** ἐσφραγίσθητε ("you were sealed") with τῷ πνεύματι…τῷ ἁγίῳ. **Four aspects of the Spirit's work** (Thielman's structure):
  1. **Seal (σφραγίζω).** Seals in Near-Eastern antiquity guaranteed quality/authenticity/ownership and prevented tampering/forgery (Fitzer TDNT). In 2 Cor. 1:22 authenticity is uppermost; here in Ephesians the orientation is **more future/eschatological** — cf. Eph. 4:30 "sealed for the day of redemption." Thielman: the seal marks God's people for **protection from the coming wrath** (Ezek. 9:4; Pss. Sol. 15.6; Rev. 7:3–8; Eph. 2:3; 5:6).
  2. **Down payment (ἀρραβών, *arrabōn*).** A Greek legal term: a partial sum guaranteeing the full amount will be paid and committing the payer to follow through (Kerr 1988). Thielman: it's the **obligation of the payer (God)** in view — the Spirit is "a sign that God will fulfill his commitment…and give them their inheritance" (cf. 2 Cor. 5:5). "The ἀρραβών metaphor…is the positive counterpart to the sealing metaphor."
  3. **In Christ (ἐν ᾧ).** Believers sealed "in whom" — the Spirit comes only within the Christ-sphere, "only insofar as they have heard and believed the gospel that redemption…comes through the sacrificial death of Jesus (v. 7)."
  4. **The promised Holy Spirit** (τῷ πνεύματι τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τῷ ἁγίῳ; genitive of quality) — fulfillment of the prophetic promise that in Israel's eschatological restoration God's Spirit would dwell among his people (Isa. 32:15; 44:3; Ezek. 36:26–27; 37:14; Joel 3:1–2; cf. Gal. 3:14; Acts 2:33).
- **[1:14]** εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆς περιποιήσεως ("for the redemption of the saved remnant"). ἀπολύτρωσις here = **future** completion of redemption (not the past redemption of v.7), evident from the down-payment logic (cf. 4:30).
- **[1:14 — crux, περιποίησις]** Thielman's distinctive reading: against the usual two options — "possession" (God's people as his possession, Exod. 19:5; 1 Pet. 2:9) or "acquisition" (believers' acquiring of salvation; Schnackenburg, Best) — he revives the rare meaning **"saved remnant / those who are saved"** (Bengel 1860; LSJ 1384, "those who are saved"). Support: pseudo-Platonic *Definitions* ("σωτηρία περιποίησις ἀβλαβής"); 2 Chron. 14:12 LXX; Heb. 10:39; 1 Thess. 5:9; 1 Pet. 2:9 / Mal. 3:17. Fits the sealing/wrath-protection context: "God gave the Holy Spirit to believers in order to seal them against destruction on the final day and for the purpose of redeeming the remnant whom he will graciously save." Confirmed by contrast in 5:6 (wrath on "sons of disobedience").
- **[1:14 Additional Note — text-critical]** Variant ὅ (neuter, agreeing with πνεύματι) vs. ὅς (masculine, agreeing with ἀρραβών). Thielman: "virtually impossible" to decide; NA27/Metzger favor ὅ, Hoehner favors ὅς. Does **not** affect meaning; the grammatical-gender question does **not** bear on the Spirit's personhood — "if the Holy Spirit can be grieved (4:30), he is a person."
- **[1:14]** Closing εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ ("for the praise of his glory") — recalls v.3 and the refrains of vv.6, 12: "He did all this 'for the praise of his glory.'"

## OVERFLOW — §III Thanksgiving & Intercession (1:15–23), subsection A (1:15–19)
*(Past briefed boundary; extracted and flagged. §III.B 1:20–23 exegesis is NOT in this slice — only announced in the intro.)*

### Intro / form (lines 420–444)
- **[1:15–23]** Greco-Roman letters often had a post-greeting prayer report (thanksgiving to the god(s) and/or intercession for the recipient's health/well-being); Pauline letters follow this, and the reports "always anticipate important themes developed in the letter body" (Schubert 1939; O'Brien 1977).
- **[form]** "Among the Pauline Letters, **only Ephesians begins with a benediction, a thanksgiving prayer report, and an intercessory prayer report.**" At the level of form Eph. 1:3–23 is closest to 2 Cor. 1:3–4, 11; at the level of prayer-report *use*, closest to **1 Thessalonians** (alternating prayer and description, concluding with prayer).
- **[structure]** Hard to tell where thanksgiving ends and intercession begins (Paul says he gives thanks, 1:16, but the following clause is intercession, 1:17–19); and where the prayer report merges into the letter body (the long relative clause 1:20–21). Paul "did not wish to distinguish carefully."
- **[themes anticipated]** 1:15–23 previews four major themes: (1) the church's defeat of hostile spiritual powers (2:2, 6; 3:10; 4:8; 6:10–17); (2) the body metaphor for the church; (3) the church full of Christ who is full of God; (4) God's power at work in his people.

### 1:15–16 — Thanksgiving for faith and love
- **[1:15]** διὰ τοῦτο κἀγώ ("because of this, I in particular") — Thielman: διὰ τοῦτο points **backward** to vv.13–14 (readers' conversion); κἀγώ = Paul's "particular interest, as the apostle to the Gentiles, in their conversion." He rejects the pseudepigraphy inference some draw from κἀγώ / borrowing from Col. 1:9 (Muddiman, Sellin, Lincoln): the phrase occurs verbatim in 1 Thess. 3:5 and fits Paul's specific Gentile-apostle self-references (Rom. 11:13–14; 15:14–16).
- **[1:15]** ἀκούσας ("after hearing") of readers' faith/love — some infer the letter can't be to Ephesus (where Paul spent 2–3 years, Acts 19–20) or is pseudepigraphic (E. Scott; Sellin). Thielman's counter: the distance is natural if Paul wrote **after 7+ years' absence and ~5 years' imprisonment** (Acts 24:27; 28:30); church membership had changed, and some believers had only loose connection to his ministry (Acts 18:24–28; Trebilco 2004). By then Paul "could have known…most of his readers only by hearing of them."
- **[1:15]** πίστις / ἀγάπη — parallel to Col. 1:4 and Philem. 5; Thielman argues the "agreement in substance but difference in specific wording" fits **one author writing all three at about the same time** better than an imitator following Colossians.
- **[1:15 faith "in the Lord Jesus"]** ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ — could be object or sphere of faith; Pauline usage favors **sphere** (people "in Christ"), but Thielman cautions against a watertight split (cf. Philem. 5 clearly object): Paul "probably intends to affirm both that his readers trusted Christ and that they are in Christ by faith."

### 1:17 — "the Spirit of wisdom and revelation"
- **[1:17]** God addressed as ὁ θεὸς τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ and ὁ πατὴρ τῆς δόξης ("the Father of glory") — "Father" metaphorical = "the origin and defining example of glory" (cf. 2 Cor. 1:3 "Father of mercies"; James 1:17 "Father of lights").
- **[1:17]** πνεῦμα σοφίας καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως — Thielman: πνεῦμα here = **God's Holy Spirit**, not a human "disposition" of wisdom (against Abbott, Westcott, Swete). Decisive point: a human "spirit of **revelation**" is "virtually unintelligible" since God gives revelation (Fee, Best); cf. 3:4–5 where the Spirit reveals the mystery. Since readers are already sealed with the Spirit (1:13), Paul prays not for the Spirit's first gift but that God "would awaken them to the Spirit's role of revealing wisdom and revelation."
- **[1:17]** ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτοῦ ("in the knowledge of him") — sphere of knowledge (of God), not means; "he prays not for knowledge generally but…the knowledge of God."

### 1:18–19 — Enlightenment; three objects of knowledge
- **[1:18a]** πεφωτισμένους ("having been enlightened") — Thielman: modifies δώῃ **adverbially** (describes what happens when God gives the Spirit: "the eyes of their heart will be enlightened"), not a second direct object (against Best) — a καί would be expected otherwise (Lincoln). The **accusative** (vs. expected dative agreeing with ὑμῖν) explained via Winer: a participle far from its governing verb "assumes an abnormal case," here anticipating the accusative ὑμᾶς of the following purpose clause.
- **[1:18a]** "eyes of the heart enlightened" — imagery common in Greco-Roman and Jewish worlds for religious insight (Ovid *Metam.* 15.60 "inner eye"; *Corpus hermeticum* 4.11b "eyes of the heart"; 1QS 2.3 "illuminate your heart"). Thielman: refers **not** to conversion (*pace* Lincoln) or baptism (*pace* Schlier) but to the Spirit's ongoing work of understanding.
- **[1:18–19]** Three indefinite (τίς) clauses, growing in complexity, the content of the prayed-for knowledge:
  - **(1) [1:18b]** ἐλπὶς τῆς κλήσεως ("the hope of his calling"). "Calling" is characteristically Pauline, at God's initiative, tied to his sovereign choice (Rom. 8:28–30; 2 Tim. 1:9). "Hope" for Paul = "not…uncertain expectation…but a firm conviction…that God will be gracious" (Rom. 4:16–18; 5:5; Col. 1:5).
  - **(2) [1:18c]** ὁ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης τῆς κληρονομίας αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις — believers are **God's own inheritance**: "God too has an inheritance, and it is his people" (οἱ ἅγιοι = all Christians). Believers "are of great value to God: they are rich in glory and they are his inheritance."
  - **(3) [1:19]** τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ ("the surpassing greatness of his power") εἰς ἡμᾶς τοὺς πιστεύοντας ("for us who believe"). Second phrase piles synonyms: κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ. Greek philosophers distinguished δύναμις (potential/capacity) from ἐνέργεια (its outworking); Paul may exploit this (cf. 3:7, 20) and prepare for 1:21 (God's power made effective in subjecting the δυνάμεις/powers to Christ). But Thielman cautions against over-parsing: "the might of his power" is a stock full expression for the greatness of God's power (1QS 11.19–20; Isa. 40:25–26 LXX; 1 Clem. 27.5). εἰς = dative of advantage; the switch from "you" to "we/us" stresses inclusiveness — "there are no exceptions."

### §III Additional Notes
- **[1:15 Additional Note — text-critical]** Whether v.15 included ἀγάπην ("love"). Earliest/best witnesses (𝔓46, א, A, B, P, 33, 1739, 1881, Origen, Jerome) **omit** love, reading "faith in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints." Best (1998) and Barth accept the shorter reading. But Thielman adopts (with hesitation) the **longer reading** (with ἀγάπην) as original, because the shorter reading forces the odd sense "faith toward all the saints" (no Pauline precedent for πίστις = mutual trust in fellow believers). Best/Barth try to rescue it by reading πίστις as "loyalty"/"love," which Thielman finds inconsistent with 1:1, 1:13. Shorter reading likely arose by scribal eye-skip between the two τήν.
- **[1:17 Additional Note]** δώῃ (subjunctive) vs. δῴη (optative). Thielman argues (minority position) for the **aorist optative δῴη**: the ἵνα is as much "that" as purpose; Paul elsewhere in Ephesians spells the aorist subjunctive δῷ (not δώῃ); Paul uses the optative of δίδωμι in prayer (Rom. 15:5); and 1 Chron. 22:12 LXX (David to Solomon, δῴη…σοφίαν καὶ σύνεσιν) is a probable model — a prayer-wish for wisdom.

## Key exegetical decisions / cruxes (summary)
1. **The 202-word single sentence (1:3–14):** Thielman treats vv.3–14 as one grammatical sentence built on the single main verb ἐξελέξατο (v.4), with everything else subordinate; four subsections A–D each ending in a "praise of his glory" refrain (vv.6, 12, 14) and joined by "in the Beloved/in whom" hinges (6b–7a, 10b–11a). Genitive strings and πρό-compounds mark the style. (Note: slice states ἐξελέξατο is the only non-subordinate verb; it does not state a specific "202-word" count — that figure in the brief is not verbatim in this slice.)
2. **ἐν ἀγάπῃ (1:4):** attaches to "holy and blameless" (ethical, anticipating 4:1ff), not to *proorisas* (v.5) — decided on the word-order rule that qualifying phrases follow their verbs.
3. **ἐν αὐτῷ (1:4):** = means/instrument (through Christ's death), not Christ's preexistence.
4. **ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει (1:8):** God's own wisdom, modifying *eperisseusen* — minority position adopted.
5. **ἀπολύτρωσις (1:7):** ransom-price metaphor "alive" but Paul's primary sense is biblical deliverance/rescue.
6. **ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι (1:10):** rhetorical "summing up/recapitulation," NOT re-creation (Jerome) or "heading up" (headship).
7. **ἐκληρώθημεν (1:11):** "made heirs," inheritance is believers'.
8. **προηλπικότας (1:12):** all Christians (not Jews/Jewish-Christians); πρό = present ("before" consummation), not past.
9. **σωτηρία (1:13) / redemption (1:14):** future-oriented, not already-completed.
10. **περιποίησις (1:14):** "saved remnant" (Bengel/LSJ minority reading), not "possession" or "acquisition."
11. **Anacoluthon (1:13):** hearing + believing + sealing = one simultaneous event.
12. **πνεῦμα (1:17):** God's Holy Spirit, not human disposition.
13. **δῴη optative (1:17):** minority reading adopted.
14. **1:15 "love":** longer reading adopted despite weaker witnesses, on internal grounds.

## Notable Greek terms with glosses
- **εὐλογητός** (*eulogētos*) — "blessed/praised" (verbal adjective, of God). **εὐλογέω/εὐλογία** — bless/blessing.
- **πνευματικός** (*pneumatikos*) — "spiritual" = from/of the Spirit. **ἐπουράνιος / ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις** — "heavenly / in the heavenly places" (dimension).
- **ἐν Χριστῷ / ἐν αὐτῷ / ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ** — "in Christ / in him / in the Beloved" (sphere).
- **ἐξελέξατο** (*exelexato*) — "he chose" (election); **πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου** — "before the foundation of the world."
- **προορίσας / προορισθέντες** (*proorisas / prooristhentes*) — "having predestined / having been predestined."
- **υἱοθεσία** (*huiothesia*) — "adoptive sonship / adoption."
- **εὐδοκία** (*eudokia*) — "good pleasure." **θέλημα** (*thelēma*) — "will." **πρόθεσις** (*prothesis*) — "purpose." **βουλή** (*boulē*) — "counsel." **ἐνεργέω/ἐνέργεια** (*energeō/energeia*) — "to work / working, effect."
- **ἀπολύτρωσις** (*apolytrōsis*) — "redemption" (ransom/deliverance). **ἄφεσις** (*aphesis*) — "forgiveness." **παραπτώματα** — "transgressions."
- **ἐπερίσσευσεν** (*eperisseusen*) — "he lavished / caused to abound." **σοφία / φρόνησις** — "wisdom / understanding."
- **μυστήριον** (*mystērion*) — "mystery" (Aramaic רָז *rāz*). **γνωρίσας** (*gnōrisas*) — "having made known."
- **οἰκονομία** (*oikonomia*) — "administration/stewardship." **πλήρωμα τῶν καιρῶν** — "fullness of the times."
- **ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι** (*anakephalaiōsasthai*) — "to sum up/recapitulate" (from κεφάλαιον "main point," not κεφαλή "head").
- **ἐκληρώθημεν** (*eklērōthēmen*) — "we were made heirs / allotted." **κληρονομία** (*klēronomia*) — "inheritance."
- **προηλπικότας** (*proēlpikotas*) — "having hoped beforehand." **ἐλπίς / κλῆσις** — "hope / calling."
- **σφραγίζω / ἐσφραγίσθητε** (*sphragizō*) — "to seal / you were sealed." **ἀρραβών** (*arrabōn*) — "down payment / earnest / pledge."
- **περιποίησις** (*peripoiēsis*) — "saved remnant" (Thielman) / "possession" / "acquisition." **σωτηρία** (*sōtēria*) — "salvation."
- **πνεῦμα σοφίας καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως** — "Spirit of wisdom and revelation." **ἐπίγνωσις** (*epignōsis*) — "knowledge." **πεφωτισμένους** (*pephōtismenous*) — "enlightened."
- **δύναμις / ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος / κράτος / ἰσχύς** — "power / surpassing greatness / might / strength."
- **δῴη / δώῃ** — optative vs. subjunctive of "may (he) give."

## Concepts fed
predestination (1:5, 11); adoption/huiothesia (1:5); election (1:4); grace/eulogia-berakah (1:3, 6, 7–8); mystērion (1:9–10); new-creation / summing-up of all things in Christ / anakephalaiōsis (1:10); Holy Spirit as seal + arrabōn + promised eschatological Spirit (1:13–14); inheritance/heirship (1:11, 14, 18); divine glory (1:6, 12, 14, 17–18); redemption/atonement-ransom debate (1:7); hope & calling (1:12, 18); Pauline authorship of Ephesians controversy (1:1, 15, text-critical notes).
